moduleMetadata.title: Password & Account Security
moduleMetadata.description: Learn how to create strong passwords, use security tools effectively, and protect your accounts from unauthorized access.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Your online accounts are often the gateway to your personal information, academic records, communications, files, and other digital resources. An attacker does not always need to break into a complicated system. Sometimes, obtaining or guessing a user's password is enough.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should understand how to create and maintain stronger and more secure accounts.

learningObjectives: Distinguish between strong and weak passwords.
Apply password length and complexity principles.
Understand the risks of password reuse.
Use password managers and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
Recognize signs of account takeover and credential theft.

sections.title: Strong vs. Weak Passwords
sections.content: A strong password is your first line of defense. Many people use weak passwords that are easy to guess or crack using automated tools.
bulletPoints: Strong: Long, unique, and complex combinations of letters, numbers, and symbols.

sections.title: The Power of Length
sections.content: Length is often more important than complexity. A longer passphrase (a string of words) can be harder for a computer to crack than a short, complex password.
sections.example: Which is stronger? 'P@ss!' or 'Correct-Horse-Battery-Staple-2026!'? The latter is much stronger due to its length.

sections.title: Password Reuse: A Dangerous Habit
sections.content: Using the same password for multiple accounts is extremely risky. If one account is compromised in a data breach, all other accounts using that password are now at risk.
sections.analogy: If you have one key for your house, car, office, and safe, losing that one key gives an attacker access to everything.

sections.title: Password Managers
sections.content: A password manager is a tool that stores and manages your passwords in an encrypted vault. You only need to remember one master password.
benefits: Generates strong, unique passwords for every site.
Alerts you to reused or weak passwords.

sections.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
sections.content: MFA adds a second layer of security. Even if an attacker has your password, they still need a second 'factor' (like a code from your phone or a fingerprint) to get in.

interactiveExercises.title: Password Strength Checker
interactiveExercises.instruction: Use the Password Strength Checker to test various passwords and see how factors like length and character variety affect the strength.

interactiveExercises.title: Build a Better Account
interactiveExercises.question: You are setting up a new professional account. Which combination offers the best security?
options: A long passphrase used only for this account + MFA.
The same password you use for your social media.
A password written on a sticky note on your monitor.
interactiveExercises.correctAnswer: A long passphrase used only for this account + MFA.
interactiveExercises.explanation: Combining uniqueness, length, and MFA provides the highest level of protection.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected MFA Alert
scenarios.content: Your phone buzzes with a verification code you didn't request, followed by a call from someone claiming to be 'IT Support' asking for the code.
scenarios.action: Do NOT share the code. IT will never ask for your MFA code or password. This is a credential theft attempt.
scenarios.lesson: MFA codes are private and should never be shared.

choices.text: Read the code aloud to the caller — they said they are IT
choices.consequence: You handed the attacker the second factor. Combined with a leaked password they may already have, they can now log into your account from their own device.

choices.text: Hang up and call IT back on the official number listed on your intranet / ID badge
choices.consequence: You broke the attacker's live session. A callback on a number you already trust confirms whether a real support case exists — IT will never ask for your MFA code.

choices.text: Make up a fake code and give it to them to waste their time
choices.consequence: You are still engaged with a social engineer. They may try a different tactic on the same call, pressure you harder, or move on to another colleague in your organization.

choices.text: Text the code to a friend to ask what to do
choices.consequence: The code is now in an unprotected message thread and visible to anyone with access to that phone. MFA codes should never leave your authenticator app.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Hang up and call IT back on the official number listed on your intranet / ID badge

scenarios.title: Urgent Deletion Warning
scenarios.content: You receive an email: 'Your account will be deleted in 10 minutes unless you click here to verify your identity.'
scenarios.lesson: Scammers use fear and urgency to make you act without thinking.

choices.text: Click the link quickly before the account is deleted
choices.consequence: The link leads to a phishing page designed to harvest your credentials. Real services do not threaten instant deletion in an email.

choices.text: Reply asking for proof that the account is real
choices.consequence: You confirm to the attacker that your mailbox is active and responsive, which puts you on a higher-value target list for future scams.

choices.text: Ignore the email and log into the service directly through its official website or app
choices.consequence: If there is a real issue, it will be visible inside the authenticated account. You bypass the email's urgency and verify through a trusted channel.

choices.text: Forward the email to coworkers to warn them
choices.consequence: Forwarding spreads the malicious link. Some recipients may click before anyone realizes it is a scam.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Ignore the email and log into the service directly through its official website or app

scenarios.title: Unrecognized Device Login
scenarios.content: You receive a legitimate alert from a service stating: 'New login detected from a Linux device in another country.'
scenarios.action: Immediately change your password and check for unauthorized changes to the account.
scenarios.lesson: Login alerts are a critical early warning system for account takeover.

choices.text: Dismiss the alert — you probably logged in from somewhere and forgot
choices.consequence: If the login is not yours, the attacker now has an active session. Ignoring the alert is the difference between stopping a takeover in minutes and discovering it in months.

choices.text: Log into the service directly (not via the alert), change your password, and review recent activity
choices.consequence: You cut off the attacker's current session, lock out anyone with your old password, and create an audit trail the service can use to investigate.

choices.text: Reply to the alert email asking for more information
choices.consequence: If the alert email is spoofed or part of a phishing chain, your reply hands an active conversation to the attacker.

choices.text: Share the alert on social media to get advice
choices.consequence: You expose details about your accounts and the incident. Attackers monitoring your profile can use those details to refine their next attempt.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Log into the service directly (not via the alert), change your password, and review recent activity

tools.name: Have I Been Pwned
tools.description: A website that allows you to check if your email address or phone number has been compromised in a known data breach.

quiz.question: Which of these is the MOST important factor for a strong password?
quiz.explanation: Length significantly increases the time it takes for automated tools to crack a password.

quiz.question: Is it safe to use the same password for your bank account and your favorite pizza shop's loyalty app?
quiz.explanation: Password reuse is a major risk. If the pizza shop has a breach, your bank account is now vulnerable.

quiz.question: What does MFA stand for?
quiz.explanation: MFA requires two or more pieces of evidence to verify a user's identity.

quiz.question: A password manager is useful because:
options: It lets you write passwords on paper.
It stores all your unique passwords in one secure place.
It makes you use '123456' for everything.
It shares your passwords with friends.
quiz.correctAnswer: It stores all your unique passwords in one secure place.
quiz.explanation: It helps maintain unique, strong passwords without needing to memorize them all.

quiz.question: What should you do if someone from 'IT' calls and asks for your MFA code to 'fix your account'?
options: Ask them to wait while you find it.
Refuse to give the code and hang up.
Email the code to them instead.
quiz.correctAnswer: Refuse to give the code and hang up.
quiz.explanation: Legitimate IT staff will never ask for your password or MFA code.

quiz.question: Which is an example of 'something you are' in MFA?
Credential theft occurs when:
options: Your computer runs out of battery.
An attacker steals your username and password.
quiz.correctAnswer: An attacker steals your username and password.
quiz.explanation: Stealing login details is the primary goal of credential theft.

quiz.question: Why are common passwords like '123456' dangerous?
options: They are the first ones attackers try using automated software.
quiz.correctAnswer: They are the first ones attackers try using automated software.
quiz.explanation: Attackers use lists of common passwords to easily compromise accounts.

keyTakeaways: Use long, unique passphrases for every account.
Use a password manager to handle unique credentials safely.
Never share MFA codes or passwords with anyone, even 'IT'.
reflectApply: Which of your accounts (Email, Bank, Social Media) currently lack MFA? Can you enable it today?
Check your most important accounts. Are any of them using the same password?
